title: Volcanoes, earthquakes, floods and cyclones: why they happen and how to stay safe
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Primary Science Stage 4, Units 4.2 'Volcanoes' and 4.3 'Earthquakes', and adds floods, cyclones and being prepared. No textbook needed.
summary: The Earth's crust is broken into giant pieces called plates, which move slowly. Where plates meet, the ground shakes and melted rock can break through. Your child models moving plates, makes a model volcano erupt, makes a book jerk forward like an earthquake, tests towers on a shaking tray, makes a tsunami wave in a tray and a whirlpool in a bottle. They find out why volcanoes also make rich soil and new land, why floods bring silt, and how warnings, strong buildings and remembered knowledge save lives, from Odisha's cyclone shelters to the island of Simeulue in 2004.
builds_on: This is the first lesson on this topic. It helps if your child knows that the Earth has layers: a thin rocky crust, a thick hot mantle, and a core at the centre. In middle school they will study plate tectonics, weather and climate in more detail.
goals: By the end your child can explain that the Earth's crust is broken into plates that move, and that most volcanoes and earthquakes happen where plates meet.
By the end your child can name the parts of a volcano and describe how magma becomes lava.
By the end your child can explain how an earthquake happens (stick and slip), and name the focus and epicentre.
By the end your child can say what to do in an earthquake, a flood, a cyclone and on seeing the sea draw back.
By the end your child can give good as well as bad effects of volcanoes and floods, and explain why the same event can be a disaster in one place and not in another.

days.title: Nature's big events, and being ready
days.goal: Share what the family knows about big natural events, and see why being ready matters.

steps.title: Have you ever...?
steps.do: Ask: 'Have you ever felt the ground shake, seen a flood, or been in a big storm? What did it feel like? Has anyone in our family?' Ask an elder to tell their story if they have one. Say: 'This week we find out why the Earth does these things, and how people stay safe.'

steps.title: Story: The Song of the Sea Running Away
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Stop when the sea pulls back and the boys run down to pick up the fish, and ask: 'What would you do? Why?' Then finish the story and ask the story questions.

steps.title: Hazard or disaster?
steps.do: Say: 'An earthquake in an empty desert hurts nobody. The same earthquake under a city of weak buildings can kill thousands. Scientists call the earthquake a hazard. It becomes a disaster when people are not protected.' Ask: 'What makes people safer?' Good answers: strong buildings, warnings, knowing what to do, high ground, help from neighbours. Ask: 'Who might be least protected?' (People in weak homes, people with no phone or radio, people who cannot move fast, and animals.)

steps.title: Start the family ready-plan
steps.do: Start the project. Together, list the events that could happen where you live (earthquake, flood, cyclone, heatwave, landslide). For each, ask: 'Where would we go? What would we take?' Begin a list for an emergency bag: water, dry food, torch, batteries, medicines, copies of documents, a whistle, phone charger, a small first-aid kit.

steps.title: One thing I will remember
steps.do: Your child writes in a notebook: 'If the ground shakes and the sea runs away, I will ____.' (Run to high ground at once.)

days.title: The moving plates of the Earth's crust
days.goal: Model the Earth's moving plates and learn what a volcano is.

steps.title: Jigsaw Earth
steps.do: Show a world map. Ask: 'Do any coastlines look as if they would fit together like jigsaw pieces?' (South America and Africa.) Say: 'The outer layer of the Earth, the crust, is broken into giant pieces called plates. They move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Millions of years ago, South America and Africa were joined.'

steps.title: Plates on a pot
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. A grown-up heats a wide pan of thick dal on a low flame until it bubbles slowly. Your child lays 3 or 4 cream crackers or thin papads on top, edges touching, like pieces of crust. Ask: 'Will the pieces stay still? What will happen at their edges?' Watch for 5 minutes without touching. Ask: 'Which pieces moved apart? Which pushed together?' (Hot dal rises from the bottom, spreads out at the top and sinks as it cools, and this carries the pieces. Hot rock deep in the Earth moves very slowly in a similar way and carries the plates.) Only the grown-up touches the stove and the pan.

steps.title: Inside a volcano
steps.do: Draw a volcano together and label: magma chamber deep below, the vent (the pipe), the crater at the top, lava flowing out, the ash cloud. Say: 'Melted rock underground is magma. When it comes out, we call it lava. It isn't fire: it is rock so hot it glows red and flows like thick honey, about 1,000 degrees Celsius.' Ask: 'Why does magma push up?' (It is hot and lighter than the solid rock around it, and full of gas, like a shaken soda bottle.)

steps.title: Volcano dance
steps.do: Play music with drums. Your child crouches as magma deep underground and rises slowly, pushing and tensing, with a quiet rumble. Then they burst up and out as an eruption, arms flung wide. Then they flow slowly as lava, moving stiffer and stiffer, until they stop still as new rock. Ask: 'What happened to the lava at the end?' (It cooled and became solid rock. This is how volcanoes make new land.)

steps.title: Active, dormant, extinct
steps.do: Say: 'Active volcanoes erupt now or erupted recently. Dormant volcanoes are sleeping and could wake. Extinct volcanoes will never erupt again. India's only active volcano is Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, which has erupted on and off since 1991.' Ask: 'Would you call a volcano that hasn't erupted for 10,000 years extinct or dormant? How sure could you be?'

need: a wide pan of thick cooked dal
a few cream crackers or thin papads

days.title: Eruptions, gifts and the Ring of Fire
days.goal: Make a volcano erupt, map where volcanoes are, and weigh their gifts against their dangers.

steps.title: Make a volcano erupt
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 on a tray, on the balcony or in the bathroom. Build a cone of damp sand or soil round a small plastic bottle. Put 2 spoons of baking soda, a drop of dish soap and a drop of red colour in the bottle. Ask: 'What will happen when the vinegar goes in? Why?' Pour in half a cup of vinegar quickly and step back. Then explain: 'Vinegar and baking soda make a gas, carbon dioxide, which pushes the liquid up and out. Real magma is full of gas too, like a shaken soda bottle, and the gas pushes it out. But real lava is melted rock, not foam.'

steps.title: The Ring of Fire
steps.do: On a world map, mark these volcanoes with red dots: Mount Fuji (Japan), Mount St Helens (USA), Popocatépetl (Mexico), Villarrica (Chile), Pinatubo (Philippines), and Krakatoa and Merapi (Indonesia). Join the dots: they make a ring round the Pacific Ocean. Say: 'About three in four of the world's active volcanoes are around the Pacific, along the edges of plates. This is called the Ring of Fire. Most big earthquakes happen there too.' Ask: 'Why do you think they line up?' (Plates meet there.) Then mark Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, which also sits where two plates meet.

steps.title: What volcanoes give
steps.do: Say: 'About 66 million years ago, huge floods of lava poured out over western India, layer after layer. The lava cooled into a dark rock called basalt, the Deccan Traps. It makes up much of Maharashtra and the hills of the northern Western Ghats. As this rock slowly broke down, it became black soil, which holds water well. Farmers in Maharashtra, north Karnataka and Telangana grow cotton, jowar and soybean on it.' List together what volcanoes give: new land (Hawaii, Iceland), rich soil, hot springs and building stone. Then list the dangers: lava, ash, poisonous gas and mudflows. Ask: 'Why do so many people live on the slopes of volcanoes like Merapi in Indonesia?' (The soil is rich, and their families have farmed there for generations.)

steps.title: Draw and label
steps.do: Your child draws and labels a volcano from memory: magma chamber, vent, crater, lava, ash. Add 'rich soil' on its slopes with tiny crops.

need: a few drops of dish soap
a world map and a red pen

days.title: Stick and slip: why the ground shakes
days.goal: Model an earthquake and see how people first detected one far away.

steps.title: Rub your hands
steps.do: Press your palms together hard and try to slide one past the other. Ask: 'Do they slide smoothly, or stick and then jump?' (They stick, then suddenly slip.) Say: 'Rocks where two plates meet do the same. A sudden slip of the rocks is an earthquake.'

steps.title: Stick and slip
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Lay a sheet of sandpaper or a rough doormat flat on the floor. Put a heavy book or a brick on it and loop a thick rubber band round it. Ask: 'When I pull the band slowly, will the book slide smoothly or jerk?' Pull the free end of the band very slowly along a ruler, and watch how far the band stretches before the book moves. Repeat five times. Ask: 'What did the book do?' (It stuck while the band stretched, jumped forward suddenly, then stuck again.) Say: 'Where two plates meet, the rocks grip each other while the plates keep moving. Strain builds up for years, like the stretched band. When the rocks slip, the ground shakes.'

steps.title: Focus, epicentre and waves
steps.do: Fill a wide steel plate with water and tap the middle of the water with a spoon. Say: 'Think of the spot you tapped as the focus, the place deep underground where the rocks slip. The spot on the surface right above the focus is the epicentre. The ripples are like seismic waves, which spread out in all directions. Shaking is strongest near the epicentre and weaker further away. Some seismic waves travel faster than others, so a far-away seismometer picks up the fast waves first.' Draw a cross-section together: a star for the focus, a dot on the surface above it for the epicentre, and rings for the waves.

steps.title: Zhang Heng's dragon jar
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v1. Zhang Heng, a scientist in China almost 1,900 years ago, built a bronze jar that showed when a far-away earthquake had happened, and in which direction. Describe the eight dragons holding balls and the eight toads below them. Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Make a seismometer
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Hang a felt pen, weighted with clay, from the top of a box on its side, so the tip just touches a strip of paper on the floor of the box. One person pulls the paper slowly while another taps the table gently, then shakes it harder. Ask: 'How do the lines change when the shaking is stronger?' (They get bigger. A real seismometer draws earthquakes in the same way.)

need: a heavy book or a brick
a thick rubber band or a strip of old cycle tube
a wide steel plate of water and a spoon
a felt pen, string and a little clay

days.title: Safe in a shake
days.goal: Test which buildings survive shaking and learn what to do in an earthquake.

steps.title: Bhuj, 2001
steps.do: Say: 'On 26 January 2001, Republic Day, a strong earthquake struck near Bhuj in Kutch, Gujarat. About 20,000 people died, most of them when buildings fell on them. The shaking itself rarely kills people. Falling buildings do.' Ask: 'So how can we save lives in an earthquake?' (Build strong buildings that can bend without falling, and know what to do when the shaking starts.)

steps.title: Shaking-table tower challenge
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Each person builds a tower at least 15 cm tall from toothpicks joined with soaked chana. Ask: 'Which tower do you think will stand? Why?' Stand each tower on the shaking tray and shake it the same way for 10 seconds. Write down whether each tower stood, leaned or fell. Then improve the towers with a wider base, triangles or cross-pieces, and test them again.

steps.title: Drop, Cover, Hold On drill
steps.do: Practise three times. Shout 'Earthquake!' Your child drops to their hands and knees, crawls under a sturdy table, and holds on to a leg with one hand while covering their head and neck with the other arm. Count 60 seconds. Say: 'Stay away from windows, mirrors and tall cupboards. If you are outside, move to an open space away from buildings, walls and wires. Don't run outside while it is shaking. Don't use a lift.' Ask: 'Where is the safest spot in each room of our house?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do the core worksheet ws1. Read the questions aloud if needed. For the two written questions, ask your child to use what they saw in the stick-and-slip test and the tower test.

need: a cup of chana soaked overnight
a tray of set agar-agar (China grass) jelly, or a tray resting on two round pencils

prep.task: Soak a cup of chana in water
Make a tray of agar-agar (China grass) jelly, or find a tray and two round pencils

days.title: Waves from the sea floor
days.goal: Make a tsunami in a tray and meet the people whose knowledge saved them in 2004.

steps.title: Tower results
steps.do: Ask: 'Which tower lasted longest on the shaking table? What made it strong?' (A wide base, triangles, things tied together, low weight on top.)

steps.title: Tsunami in a tray
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. In a long baking tray or plastic box, pile sand at one end to make a sloping beach. Pour water into the other end until it is about 3 cm deep. Lay a flat plastic lid on the bottom in the deep water. Ask: 'If the sea floor jumps up, where will the wave be tallest: in the deep water or at the beach?' Quickly lift one edge of the lid by about a centimetre, like the sea floor jumping in an earthquake. Watch the wave cross the tray and grow taller at the beach. Then lift the lid slowly. Ask: 'Why did the slow lift make almost no wave?' (A tsunami needs the sea floor to move suddenly.)

steps.title: 26 December 2004
steps.do: Say gently: 'On the morning of 26 December 2004, one of the biggest earthquakes ever recorded, about magnitude 9.1, happened under the sea near Sumatra in Indonesia. The sea floor jumped up and lifted the ocean above it. Tsunami waves raced across the Indian Ocean as fast as a jet plane. They reached the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Sri Lanka and even Africa. About 230,000 people died, including more than 10,000 in India. On the mainland, Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu was hit hardest.' Pause and let your child ask anything. Say: 'Since 2007, India has had a tsunami warning centre in Hyderabad that watches the ocean day and night.'

steps.title: The song and the forest
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v3: the people of Simeulue, an island near Sumatra, and the Onge people of Little Andaman. Then tell the true story of Tilly Smith, a 10-year-old English girl on a beach in Thailand that morning. She saw the sea drawing back, remembered her geography lesson about tsunamis, and warned her parents. The beach was cleared before the wave came. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The signs of a tsunami
steps.do: Make a sign for the family ready-plan: 'TSUNAMI SIGNS: a strong or long earthquake near the coast; the sea suddenly running away or rising; a loud roar from the sea. WHAT TO DO: go to high ground or far inland at once. Don't wait for a warning. Don't go to look. Stay away until told it is safe: the waves come again and again.'

need: a long baking tray or plastic box
a small flat plastic lid or ruler

days.title: Rivers rise and winds spin
days.goal: Find out why rivers flood, how cyclones form, and how Odisha learned to save lives.

steps.title: Animals and earthquakes
steps.do: Ask first: 'Have you heard that animals know when an earthquake is coming? How could we test it?' Then tell your child about Voice v2: scientists in Italy put motion sensors on cows, sheep and dogs on a farm to find out whether the animals sense an earthquake before it starts. Share what they found, and why other scientists are not yet convinced. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: A tornado in a bottle
steps.do: Do Experiment e5 over a sink. Fill one bottle two-thirds with water. Put an empty bottle upside down on top, mouth to mouth, and tape them together tightly. Ask: 'Will the water drain faster if we swirl it?' Turn the bottles over and time how long the water takes to drain. Then turn them over again, swirl the top bottle in quick circles, and time it again. Ask: 'What shape did the spinning water make?' (A funnel with a hollow middle, called a vortex. A cyclone is spinning air, and it also has a calm middle.)

steps.title: How a cyclone grows
steps.do: Say: 'Cyclones form over warm seas, like the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. Warm, wet air rises, and more air rushes in to take its place. Because the Earth spins, the air rushing in starts to turn, round and round, faster and faster. In the middle is the calm eye, and around it is a wall of the fiercest wind and rain. Chennai and the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are often hit by cyclones from the Bay of Bengal between October and December.' Ask: 'Why do cyclones weaken when they reach land?' (They lose the warm sea water that feeds them.)

steps.title: Odisha, 1999 and 2013
steps.do: Say: 'In October 1999 a super cyclone hit Odisha. There were few warnings and few shelters, and about 10,000 people died. Odisha then built hundreds of cyclone shelters, trained volunteers in every village, and learned to warn and move people fast. In October 2013, Cyclone Phailin, nearly as strong, hit the same coast. About a million people were moved to safety in two days, and fewer than 50 died.' Ask: 'What changed: the cyclone or the people?'

steps.title: Storm symphony
steps.do: Make a storm with what you have: fingers tapping a table for rain, a steel plate shaken for thunder, blowing for wind, then sudden silence for the eye, then the storm again from the other side. Ask: 'Why does the wind come from the other side after the eye passes?' (The storm is spinning; the other side of the wheel blows the opposite way.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child begins the stretch worksheet ws2. Read the questions aloud if needed. They can finish it tomorrow.

need: two clear plastic bottles of the same size

days.title: Floods, the ready-plan and teaching it back
days.goal: Find out why rivers flood and what floods give, play the ready game, and finish the family plan.

steps.title: Floods: harm and gift
steps.do: Ask first: 'Why do you think rivers flood?' Then say: 'A river floods when more water comes than its channel can hold, from heavy monsoon rain, melting snow or a cyclone's rain. The flat land a river spreads over in a flood is called its floodplain. Floods also carry silt, a fine mud that makes farmland rich. The plains of the Ganga and the Brahmaputra were built this way. Floods do the most harm where people build on floodplains and lakes, cover the ground with concrete, block drains or cut forests. In 2015 Chennai flooded badly, partly because homes had been built over its lakes and marshes. In the 2018 Kerala floods, fishermen brought their boats and rescued tens of thousands of people.' Ask: 'What should you never do in a flood?' (Walk or drive through flowing water, touch electric wires, or drink floodwater.)

steps.title: Ready! cooperative game
steps.do: Play the card game g1 together. Everyone is on one team against the events. Turn over an event card, and together choose the right action cards and say why, within one minute.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the challenge worksheet ws3, and finishes ws2 if needed. Ask for reasons on the written questions, not just answers.

steps.title: End check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud, one at a time. After each answer, ask 'Why?' and praise good reasons, not just right answers.

steps.title: Teach it back and finish the ready-plan
steps.do: Your child finishes the project and presents the family ready-plan to everyone at home: what to do in an earthquake, a flood, a cyclone and on seeing tsunami signs, where the emergency bag is, and the family meeting place. Then they explain, with a drawing, how moving plates cause earthquakes and volcanoes.

experiments.title: Plates on a pot
experiments.question: How do the pieces of the Earth's crust move?
need: a wide pan of thick cooked dal
3 or 4 cream crackers or thin papads
steps: A grown-up heats the pot of thick dal gently until it starts to bubble slowly, then turns the flame very low.
Lay the crackers gently on top, edges touching, like a cracked crust.
Watch closely for 5 minutes without touching. Look at the edges of the crackers.
Turn off the flame and let it cool before eating!
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the crackers stay still? What will happen at their edges?'
experiments.observe: The crackers slowly drift. Some move apart and dal oozes up between them; some push together and tilt up or slide under each other.
experiments.why: The hot dal at the bottom rises, spreads out at the top and sinks again as it cools, slowly carrying the crackers. Deep in the Earth, the hot mantle rock moves very, very slowly in a similar way, and the plates of crust move a few centimetres a year. Where plates pull apart, magma rises to fill the gap; where they push together, mountains rise, volcanoes form and earthquakes shake.
experiments.safety: Only a grown-up touches the stove and pot. Hot dal can bubble and spit: keep faces back and hands away.

experiments.title: Make a volcano erupt
experiments.question: What makes a volcano erupt?
need: damp sand or soil to build a cone around it
a few drops of dish soap
steps: Stand the bottle on the tray and build a volcano-shaped cone of damp sand or soil round it, leaving the mouth open.
Put the baking soda, a drop of soap and colouring into the bottle.
Pour in the vinegar quickly and step back.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen when the vinegar meets the soda? Why?'
experiments.observe: Foam rushes up the bottle and pours out of the top and down the sides.
experiments.why: Vinegar and baking soda react and make carbon dioxide gas very fast. The gas needs room, so it pushes the liquid up and out. In a real volcano, magma is full of dissolved gases, like a shaken soda bottle. As it rises and the pressure drops, the gas comes out as bubbles and drives the magma up and out. This models the push of the gas, not real lava, which is melted rock at about 1,000 °C.
experiments.safety: Do it on a tray, on the balcony or in the bathroom. Keep vinegar away from eyes, and wash hands after.

experiments.title: Stick and slip
experiments.question: Why do earthquakes happen suddenly, not smoothly?
need: a heavy book or a brick
a sheet of sandpaper or a rough doormat
a thick rubber band or a strip of old cycle tube
steps: Lay the sandpaper or doormat flat. Put the book on it and loop the rubber band round the book.
Pull the free end of the band very slowly and steadily along the ruler.
Watch the book and the band. Measure how far the band stretches before the book moves.
Repeat five times. Does the book ever slide smoothly?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the book slide smoothly as you pull, or jerk?'
experiments.observe: The band stretches while the book sticks. Then the book suddenly jumps forward, the band goes slack, and the book sticks again. It moves in jerks.
experiments.why: Where two plates meet, the rocks grip each other by friction while the plates keep moving, so strain builds up, like the stretched band, for years or centuries. When the rocks can't hold any more, they slip suddenly, and the stored energy shakes the ground as an earthquake. Then they stick again and the strain starts building once more.
experiments.safety: Pull slowly; a snapping rubber band can sting. Keep faces away.

experiments.title: Tsunami in a tray
experiments.question: How does a movement of the sea floor make a tsunami?
need: a long baking tray or plastic box
a flat plastic lid or ruler
steps: Pile sand at one end to make a sloping beach. Pour water gently into the other end until it is about 3 cm deep.
Lay the lid flat on the bottom in the deep water.
Lift one edge of the lid up quickly by a centimetre, like the sea floor jumping in an earthquake.
Watch the wave reach the beach. Look at the water at the beach just before the wave arrives.
Try lifting it slowly. Is the wave different?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the wave be big in the deep water or when it reaches the beach?'
experiments.observe: A low, wide wave travels across the tray and grows taller as it reaches the shallow beach. A slow lift makes almost no wave.
experiments.why: When the sea floor jumps suddenly, it lifts all the water above it. That bulge spreads out as waves. In the deep ocean a tsunami is low and very fast, as fast as a jet plane. Near the coast, in shallow water, it slows down and piles up into a wall of water. Sometimes the sea first runs away from the beach before the wave comes. That is a warning to run to high ground at once.
experiments.safety: Mop up spills so nobody slips.

experiments.title: A tornado in a bottle
experiments.question: How do spinning storms work?
need: two clear plastic bottles of the same size
glitter or a few drops of food colouring (optional)
steps: Fill one bottle about two-thirds with water and add glitter.
Put the empty bottle upside down on top, mouth to mouth, and tape them together very tightly.
Turn them over so the water is on top. Watch.
Now turn them over again and swirl the top bottle in quick circles, then hold it still.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the water drain faster with or without the swirl?'
experiments.observe: Without a swirl, the water glugs slowly. With a swirl, a spinning funnel, a vortex, forms in the middle and the water drains quickly through it.
experiments.why: Once the water is spinning, it spirals into a funnel with a hollow middle, so air can come up while water goes down. Tornadoes and cyclones are spinning air, not water, but they share this shape: a fast-spinning wall around a calm centre. A cyclone's eye is that centre, many kilometres wide.
experiments.safety: Tape the bottles firmly. Do it over a sink or outdoors.

activities.title: Make a seismometer
need: a cardboard box with the top cut off, on its side
a little clay or a stone to weigh the pen
a long strip of paper (join A4 sheets)
steps: Tie the pen, weighted with clay, to a string and hang it from the top of the box so its tip just touches the floor of the box.
Feed the paper strip through the bottom of the box under the pen tip.
One person pulls the paper slowly through while another gently taps the table, then shakes it harder.
Compare the lines: a quiet day, a small tremor, a big shake.
activities.outcome: A paper record with wiggly lines that get bigger with stronger shaking: how seismometers draw earthquakes.

activities.title: Shaking-table tower challenge
need: a tray of set agar-agar (China grass) jelly, or a tray resting on two round pencils
steps: Each person builds a tower at least 15 cm tall from toothpicks, joined with soaked chana.
Stand the tower on the jelly or the tray. Shake it for 10 seconds, the same way for each tower.
Record: did it stand, lean or fall?
Improve your tower: try a wider base, triangles, cross-braces. Test again.
Which changes helped most?
activities.outcome: Your child discovers that wide bases, triangles and tied-together frames resist shaking, the same ideas engineers use for earthquake-safe buildings.

project.title: Our family ready-plan
steps: List the events that could happen where you live.
For each, write what to do and where to go.
Pack, or list, an emergency bag: water, dry food, torch, batteries, medicines, copies of documents, whistle, charger, first-aid kit.
Choose a family meeting place outside the home and one further away.
Write emergency numbers on a card (112 is India's all-in-one emergency number).
Present it to the family.
project.outcome: A real, practical plan your family keeps, made by your child.

game.title: Ready!
rules: Cut out the cards. Put the EVENT cards in one pile and deal the ACTION cards out to everyone.
Turn over an event card and read it aloud.
Players together must lay down the right action card(s) for it, explaining why, within one minute (count aloud).
If you manage it, the event is 'survived': put it in the safe pile. If not, it goes in the 'disaster' pile.
Everyone wins together if the safe pile is bigger. Shuffle and play again: can you beat your score?

big: Is an earthquake bad in itself, or only when it hurts people and other living beings?
Should people be allowed to build homes on floodplains and volcano slopes? Who should decide?
Old songs saved a whole island in 2004. What knowledge do the elders in your family hold that might one day save someone?
If we can't stop nature's events, what can we change?

challenge.q: 'In an earthquake, stand in a doorway.' Should you?
challenge.hint: This was old advice from the days of adobe houses in America. In modern homes, doorways are not stronger than other parts, and a swinging door can hurt you. Safety experts now advise Drop, Cover, Hold On under a sturdy table. Why might old advice keep spreading even after it changes?

There are no flames. Lava is melted rock glowing red- or yellow-hot, about 700 to 1,200 °C. The 'smoke' is mostly ash (tiny bits of rock and glass) and gases like steam. Sometimes things near lava catch fire.

Scientists can say where earthquakes are likely and roughly how often, but not exactly when. In 1975 in Haicheng, China, people were moved out after warning signs and many were saved; but the next year, in Tangshan, there was no warning and a huge number of people died. Most experts think reliable short-term prediction is not possible yet, which is why strong buildings and quick warnings matter.

perspectives.view: If a river could speak, she might say: 'I am not flooding your land. You built your houses on my floodplain, the land I spread over when the monsoon gives me too much water. My floods carried the silt that made your fields.' Ask: who was there first?

Farmers on the slopes of volcanoes like Merapi in Java and Etna in Sicily stay because the soil is so rich, and many watch the mountain closely and honour it. Ask: is it foolish or wise to live beside a volcano?

Studies of many disasters, including the 2004 tsunami, found that more women than men died in some places, partly because fewer women had been taught to swim or climb, and many stayed back to look for children and elders. Ask: why do skills like swimming matter for everyone? Who should learn them?

voices.idea: In 132 CE he built a bronze earthquake detector: a jar with eight dragons round it, each holding a ball, above eight open-mouthed toads. When the ground shook from a distant earthquake, a ball dropped from one dragon into a toad, showing the direction. The official history of the Han dynasty records that in 138 CE a ball dropped when nobody felt anything, and days later a messenger arrived reporting an earthquake far to the west, in Longxi.
voices.then: At first people at court doubted it, until the messenger came.
voices.now: Historians accept that he built the device and the record is real. No original survives, and exactly how it worked inside is still debated; modern reconstructions use a pendulum. Modern seismometers came about 1,700 years later.
voices.ask: The court only believed Zhang Heng when the messenger arrived. Why is a prediction that comes true so convincing? Could it ever be luck?

voices.who: Martin Wikelski and colleagues (2020), Max Planck Institute, Germany
voices.idea: They fitted motion sensors to cows, sheep and dogs on a farm in an earthquake area of Italy and reported that the animals became unusually restless in the hours before some earthquakes, more so the closer they were to the epicentre.
voices.then: There are stories from many cultures, including from China and India, of animals behaving strangely before earthquakes. Many scientists think these stories are remembered only when an earthquake follows, and forgotten when it doesn't.
voices.now: The 2020 study is interesting but small, over a few months on one farm. Most earthquake scientists say there is not yet good evidence that animals can reliably sense earthquakes before they start, and nobody knows what they would be sensing.
voices.ask: If your dog barked strangely and then an earthquake came, would that prove dogs can sense earthquakes? How many times would you need to see it, and what else would you need to count?

voices.who: The people of Simeulue Island, Indonesia, and the Onge of Little Andaman, India (2004)
voices.idea: On Simeulue, very close to the 2004 earthquake, a terrible tsunami in 1907 had been remembered in stories and lullabies called smong: if the ground shakes hard and the sea runs away, run to the hills; don't wait. In 2004 islanders ran, and reports say only about seven of about 78,000 people died. On Little Andaman, the Onge, who have lived there for thousands of years, are reported to have moved to high ground after the earthquake, and almost all of the roughly 100 Onge survived; their oral traditions are believed to have warned them.
voices.then: Many outsiders had thought of such knowledge as just 'old stories'. Scientists who studied Simeulue after 2004 were amazed.
voices.now: Researchers now study and teach oral warning traditions as part of disaster safety. The Simeulue numbers are well recorded; the exact details of what the Onge knew and did are less certain, because they were reported by outsiders.
voices.ask: Stories and lullabies carried a scientific warning for almost 100 years. Is a song a kind of science? What makes knowledge survive?

check.q: What are plates, and what happens where they meet?
check.a: Giant pieces of the Earth's crust that move slowly. Where they meet, there are earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

check.q: What is the difference between magma and lava?
check.a: Magma is melted rock underground; lava is melted rock that has come out on the surface.
Rocks along a crack grip each other while the plates keep moving, strain builds up, and then they slip suddenly, shaking the ground.
The place on the surface right above where the earthquake starts (the focus).

check.q: What should you do if you are indoors in an earthquake?
check.a: Drop, Cover, Hold On under a sturdy table, away from windows.

check.q: What are the warning signs of a tsunami, and what do you do?
check.a: A strong earthquake near the coast, the sea running away or a roar from the sea. Go to high ground at once.

check.q: Give one good effect of volcanoes or floods.
check.a: Rich soil (Deccan black soil), new land, silt on farmland, hot springs.

check.q: Why did far fewer people die in Odisha's 2013 cyclone than in 1999?
check.a: Better warnings, cyclone shelters and moving about a million people to safety.

story.title: The Song of the Sea Running Away
text: On Simeulue, the island where I was born, off the coast of Sumatra, every child knows a song. Our grandmothers sing it to us when we are too small to remember learning it. It is not a happy song or a sad one. It is just a song, sung slowly, on the veranda in the evenings, while the frogs croak in the paddy fields.
It goes something like this: when the ground shakes hard, and the sea runs away, do not wait, do not look. Run to the hills. The smong is coming.

Smong is our word for the great wave. My grandmother's grandmother saw it, in 1907, when it came out of the sea and swallowed the villages. In those days, the song says, when the sea ran away, people ran down onto the sand to pick up the fish that were flopping on the bare reef. And then the smong came back.

I always thought it was just a song, the way the song about the crocodile in the river is just a song. I was nine years old, and nothing ever happened on our island except rain and coconuts and school.
It was a Sunday morning, the day after Christmas, though we don't keep Christmas on our island. I was helping my mother hang out the washing when the ground began to move.

It did not shake the way the ground sometimes trembles, a little rattle and done. It rolled. It swayed, like the deck of my uncle's boat, on and on, so long that I fell over on the grass and the washing line twanged and the coconut palms swung like crazy dancers. My mother held me and we lay on the ground and the earth went on rolling under us, for what felt like many minutes. I could hear pots crashing inside the house, and dogs howling, and a goat screaming.
Then it stopped.

Everything was very quiet. Some of the houses had cracks. Old Pak Rahman's kitchen had fallen down. But nobody was hurt. People came out of their houses, laughing a little, the way you laugh when you are frightened and then you are not.
Then my cousin Dedi shouted from the beach. "Look! Look at the sea!"

We ran to the edge of the trees. The sea had gone. Not gone completely: it was there, far, far out, a grey line. But between us and it was bare reef and sand, wet and shining, a whole new land that had never been seen before, with pools full of trapped fish leaping and flashing silver in the sun. Some of the bigger boys whooped and started running down onto the reef, with buckets.
I stood very still. The sun was warm. The fish were beautiful. And in my head, very quietly, in my grandmother's voice, the song began to sing itself.
When the ground shakes hard. And the sea runs away. Do not wait. Do not look.
My body understood before I did. The shaking had been under the sea. Something down there had moved, and pulled the water away, and the water would come back.
"SMONG!" I screamed. I had never screamed so loud in my life. "SMONG! SMONG! RUN TO THE HILLS!"

For one moment everyone looked at me, a skinny girl with a wet sarong in her hand. And then the word went through them like a wind. One old woman shouted it, then my mother, then everyone. "Smong!" The boys dropped their buckets and ran back up the beach. Mothers grabbed babies. Pak Rahman, who could hardly walk, was lifted onto my uncle's back. Nobody stopped to fetch anything. Nobody waited for a siren, because there was no siren. We ran up the path behind the village into the forest, up and up the steep hill, slipping on roots, pulling each other, until we were high among the clove trees and could run no more.
From there we turned and looked.

The sea came back. It did not come as a curling wave like the ones the surfers ride. It came as a wall, grey-brown and roaring, wider than the whole bay, carrying trees and boats inside it. It poured over the beach where the fish had been. It poured over the washing line, and our house, and the school, and the mosque, and went on far inland. Then it drew back. And then it came again.

My mother held my hand so tightly it hurt. I did not cry. I was too busy counting. My grandmother. My little brother. Dedi. The boys with the buckets. Pak Rahman. One by one, I found them all among the trees.

When we went down, three days later, our village was mud and broken wood. Our house was gone. My school was gone. But we were there to see it. Across the whole island, the grown-ups said afterwards, almost everyone had run to the hills. Of all the tens of thousands of people on Simeulue, only a handful were lost.
Scientists came later, from far away, with notebooks and cameras. They asked us how we knew. We sang them the song.
story.epiphany: A tsunami is made when an earthquake under the sea suddenly moves the sea floor; often the water first runs away from the shore, and that is the signal to run to high ground at once. The turn comes when the narrator, seeing the fish on the bare reef, remembers the smong song and understands that the shaking under the sea has pulled the water back and it will return. The story is fiction, but it is built on the real Simeulue tradition that saved almost everyone on the island in 2004, nearly a hundred years after the 1907 tsunami that taught it.
ask: Why did the boys run down onto the reef?
What did the song tell the girl to do, and why was it right?
Why didn't the islanders wait for a siren?
How had the song been kept alive for almost 100 years?
The scientists asked the islanders how they knew. What could scientists learn from them?

ideas.idea: The ground under us is slowly moving.
ideas.more: The plates of the Earth's crust move a few centimetres a year. Where they pull apart, push together or grind past each other, the ground shakes, mountains rise and volcanoes form. Plates pushing together made the Himalaya.

ideas.idea: Nature's events give as well as take.
ideas.more: Lava builds new land, volcanic rock becomes rich soil, floods spread fertile silt. They become disasters when people are in harm's way without protection.

ideas.idea: Knowledge, warnings and neighbours save more lives than anything else.
ideas.more: Strong buildings, cyclone shelters, a tsunami warning centre, earthquake drills and even an old lullaby have saved many thousands of people. Being ready is something a family and a town can do together.

unknowns: Can earthquakes ever be predicted to the day? Scientists are still searching for reliable warning signs, and many doubt it is possible.
What exactly triggers a volcano to erupt at a particular moment, after sleeping for years or centuries? Scientists watch for signs, but each volcano behaves differently.
How will a warming ocean change cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea? Many scientists find they are becoming stronger and wetter, but how much is still debated.
